utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It looks as though there are no questions from any other Defence counsel; and, therefore, you're about to be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply throughout your evidence. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999, during the NATO intervention, you were in charge of morale and information for -- for the brigade, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for information, not informatics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what rank were you then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it from paragraph 19 of your statement, in which you take issue with Nik Peraj, you're saying that you also had responsibility for barrack security. What was your role in barrack security?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to my regular duties as officer for morale and information, I had additional tasks. One of them was to be responsible for the security of the barracks located in the centre of the town. I was responsible for guarding it. It was an abandoned barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And during the intervention, that barracks was the cultural centre in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That barracks is next to the cultural hall in Djakovica; ten metres away, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the guards to the barracks were billeted there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was outside security of the barracks. It was about guarding the barracks from any outsiders who may come in and take things from inside; non-combat equipment, blankets, and other property that the unit left there when they left their peacetime location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. But the guards for the barracks, those people, your staff involved in guarding the barracks, were lodged at the barracks. That is where they had their sleeping quarters. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We slept in a dugout. I slept together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, apart from the -- your responsibilities as chief of information and morale, and also additionally guarding the barracks, did you have any other responsibilities during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of my duties to contact with local authorities on orders of the brigade commander, if he would give me one or another task, and to give them assistance if they requested it from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Nik Peraj also had responsibilities in respect to guarding the barracks. Do you know if he had other responsibilities? Well, for one, you know he was also responsible for transporting the bodies of VJ soldiers to places of burial, from hospital to the places of burial. You know that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Nik Peraj did have that responsibility you mentioned. He participated with me in touring the barracks, and he helped me with the transport of the wounded members of our unit up to Nis and dealing with their funeral arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he have any other responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You -- you don't know about anything, any responsibilities he had in respect to the security section?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not issue him with any assignments. He was subordinated to the operations organ of the brigade. That means he was not directly subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could the cultural centre or did the cultural centre, during the intervention, and the barracks ten metres beside, accommodate all the personnel that had tasks in your brigade, or were some personnel accommodated elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part where I was, and Nik Peraj, there was also Major Zivkovic and two and three soldiers, and that was all located in the cultural hall. The second part of the brigade command was located in other facilities; in the basement of the department store, for instance, and in some other buildings that were abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one intervention for the record. Line 24, it says "in other buildings that were abandoned." The witness said "other socially owned facilities that were abandoned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were units of the brigade sometimes accommodated in private houses?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that units of the brigade were based in private houses, because our brigade was one of anti-aircraft defence. Those were units that had self-propelled weapons, and they were located across the territory in their positions. So they were unable to be in houses. They had to be next -- they had to man their weapons. If possible, crews were even quartered inside their equipment. If possible, they spent all their time there, worked there, slept there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So were these units that you speak of, that had their weapons and had to man their equipment, were these accommodated in socially owned facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the unit were placed in socially owned facilities such as Sokara and Bambi, in some depots and warehouses, but the units that I toured I did not find in private houses. I'm speaking only about the units that I inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know Marsenic's house? Maybe I have the pronunciation incorrect. Probably, I have the pronunciation incorrect, but do you know Marsenic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of Marsenic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I probably -- if I could show you a document, you might be able to get the pronunciation right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I have a look at P1086, and this in a war diary of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at an entry for the 1st of April, 1999, at 0845 hours, and that's at page 9 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S. There's a sentence near the end of the entries for the 1st of April, you'll see, that speaks about events between 1800 and 2100 hours. You see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read it, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From 1800 to 2100 hours, on orders of the brigade commander, the command post was transferred from Marsenic house to the cultural house of Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what Marsenic -- Marsenic's house was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really don't know what Marsenic house is. I'm not familiar with that. I went straight from the barracks to the cultural centre. I never went to Marsenic house. I'm not familiar with that surname or the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You would not know, I take it, since Nik Peraj was directly subordinated to operations and not to you, whether or not he may have had other responsibilities that he was assigned to with units that were located in houses like Marsenic houses -- house, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. It was not my job to issue him with assignments, and he didn't tell me what assignments he had got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, therefore, you wouldn't know whether or not what he said at paragraph 62 of his statement, that there was a house where his section lived, is correct or incorrect. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nik Peraj and I were at the cultural centre together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do we know what Marsenic house is? Is there any evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it has been identified. I think it hasn't been shown to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Likewise, I would like to know what is Bambi and Sokara said earlier by the witness. What he means by socially owned houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you -- you heard His Honour. May I just find the reference to Bambi first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, you identified some of the socially owned facilities as named Sokara and Bambi. What are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. One is a factory producing fruit juice called Bambi. It was part of the complex Bambi from Pozarevac. It was bottling fruit juice and wine, and it was at the exit of Djakovica town. It had empty warehouses that the army moved into, so that they wouldn't have to move into private houses and buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about Sokara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sokara is a fruit bottling and drinks bottling facility. That was the local name for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would not know, would you, sir, where any other unit that Nik Peraj might have had to work with was housed, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nik Peraj also worked with that unit alone, not with other units, as far as I know. He only worked on the security of that barracks in town. He didn't work with other units. It was not his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as far as you know, do --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you don't know what he might have been tasked to do by the section that he was directly subordinate to on every occasion during the intervention, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this witness has clearly answered this question twice. He knows that Nik Peraj worked with that unit alone and he knows nothing else, and he also slept in the same quarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, there's nothing inappropriate about this cross-examination, bearing in mind the importance of the issue. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You told us earlier that you were not his direct superior. He was subordinate to a different section. You're not in a position to say, sir, what tasks he had every day during the NATO intervention, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position to tell you. I know only about those of his assignments that I was aware of, such as transporting dead army members. I had no right and no time to question him as to what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in -- to move on, in your recitation of what Nik Peraj said at paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 21 of your statement, you said that one of -- one of the things that indicates that Nik Peraj's lying is that, in his statement at paragraph 67, he said that he spent the night at the cultural centre. Now, I checked paragraph 67 of Nik Peraj's statement, and he said that on the night of the 26th -- well, in paragraph 66, he said on the night of 26th, he was in Vucitrn municipality; and in paragraph 67, he that he arrived at the cultural centre the next day, the 27th, at 1130 hours and slept there until 1400 hours. That is what is recorded in statement in paragraph 67. He did not sleep at the cultural centre that night. He was not there in the course of the day for three or four hours. Did you actually read Nik Peraj's statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the Prosecutor is not quoting well from the statement of Nik Peraj of the 8th and 9th August, 2006, where it says in the second sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's have it on the screen. What is its number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we wish paragraph 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the Serbian and the English version are identical. It is the two first sentences that are relevant, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where's the reference to "sleeping"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I request that the witness be given the Serbian version in e-court. I will read it to you: "At 11.30 ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Vintar, on the left of the screen, you should have your own statement and paragraph 21. No, no. Please go back to Mr. Vintar's own statement, paragraph 21, which I think was on the screen. Was that just delayed action and we can't do that, perhaps, on the technology? You have your statement in front of you, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you see the reference to paragraph 67. If you look at paragraph 21 of your own statement, you've got it in paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, you refer to paragraph 67 of the statement of Nik Peraj. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you read that line. Just read the few words before "(Paragraph 67)". Just read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, if you look at other parts of his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just read the few words before the words ("Paragraph 67)." There's a comma about six words earlier. Read from that comma.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When he returned from the assignment of transporting the dead members of the VJ, he came to the cultural centre where part of the command headquarters of the brigade was located and spent the night there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you'd now look at paragraph 67 of the statement of Nik Peraj, which will be put on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, just be patient, please. Be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is with the translation, or the interpretation it, because it says "spent the night there," and the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And hopefully that's reliable. I have it in writing here in this statement. We've just heard it, and the interpreter has twice told us it says "spent the night."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is insisting that it says "slept." The interpreter said "spent the night." It may make a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will need to have this formally translated, then, by CLSS. I find it difficult to see that there should be confusion between these two expressions. There certainly wouldn't in the English language. Perhaps, there is some peculiarity in Serbian that makes these two expressions identical, but I find that difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, even the meaning -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am astonished at this linguistic difficulty, because there is no relationship between spending the night and sleeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can be wide awake all night. Now, so you can understand my difficulty in the two versions of the translation that are being offered. They can't possibly both be right. So we will get it formally translated by CLSS. Mr. Stamp, you will have to tiptoe around your cross-examination of this, bearing in mind the possibility of two different translations of what was said by the witness about Peraj's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You now have paragraph 67 of Peraj's statement on the screen. Could you read the beginning of that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At 1130 hours, I went to the cultural centre in Djakovica. The army of Yugoslavia put up its headquarters in the cultural centre because that was one of the safest places. I slept in the cultural centre until 1400 hours, and then I went to the Catholic church near Boris Kidric Street to fetch my family. "I went there together with my brother ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that what you are referring to in paragraph 21 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just go back for a moment to my own paragraph 21, if that's not a problem, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there I meant what Nik Peraj said, where he said that we would meet in some house, he and I, and that I made some sort of lists there; whereas, I was in the cultural centre together with him and he was in the cultural centre together with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the real issue is -- well, is the issue over the day or the night-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, Peraj was on that assignment when somebody who was killed and transported dead and -- from Nis. And when I think back, I know that he returned that day. Whether he slept there or not, I can't remember. Probably he had a rest, because he had a very tiring journey. He was transporting dead army members to Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is abundantly clear is that the passage we're talking about only covers a period of two and a half hours. That may not matter all this debate. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The passage in Nik Peraj's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I referred to the passage in paragraph 66 first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 66 of his statement, he said that he spent the night of the 26th at Priluzje village in Vucitrn, and left on the morning of the 27th and arrived in Djakovica at 11.00 in the morning; and in paragraph 67, he says, at 11.30 hours, he went to the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but paragraph 21 in this witness's statement is talking about the night of the -- if he's talking about night at all, it would be talking about the next night. It would appear he's not talking about the night, from what we're being told. [Priluzje].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 21 reads that Nik Peraj claimed that on the 27th of April, when he returned from a task transporting dead VJ members, he came to cultural centre where part of the command was located, and that he spent the night there, and he refers to paragraph 67 to support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, but the paragraph 66 you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is the night of the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is the night of the 26th. It's a different night, and it may not matter because all that he, Peraj, is claiming is to have slept for two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it really boils down to a matter for the trier of fact to conclude, but what the witness, without addressing, is saying is that Peraj, in paragraph 67 - of this statement he makes in paragraph 67 - shows that he's not the speaking truth because he says he spent the night, and he doesn't say that in paragraph 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your point, Mr. Stamp, and I doubt if further explanation with the witness is going to make it any witness any clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were giving this statement, Mr. Vintar, were you shown Peraj's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can see that there's a problem here. Might I be allowed to say just one word? I'm talking about the fact that in the previous paragraph, I don't know what number it is, but if you show me my statement I'll be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your statement, you should have there in front of you. Do you not have a written copy in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately not. Unfortunately not. Your Honour, may we please go back to paragraph 20 of my statement, because in that paragraph, on the basis of Nik Peraj's statement, in paragraph 62, who claims that right before the action in Meje, he was put up with his unit in a house which belonged to an Albanian, and where allegedly the massacre in Meje was planned, then I follow on from that and I say that that is not correct, that we were actually in the cultural centre. Then in paragraph 21, I continue to explain the situation. Then if we were to go on further, Nik Peraj claims that that night, the 27th of April, at 10.00, he saw that I was writing a report, a list of those who were killed in the cultural centre. But I have to tell you that after 2200 hours in the evening, he didn't have the right to leave the cultural centre facility or any other facility where he happened to be, because that was the order that had been given. So we were in the cultural centre, and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, are you claiming your understanding of his statement is also that he spent the night of the 27th in the cultural centre? And by "the night," I mean from 1800 hours to 0600 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this distance and the passage of time, I can say that I'm not quite sure but that I'm almost 80 per cent convinced that he was there, that we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't have anywhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question. Listen to the question. Are you claiming it's your understanding that, in his statement, he said that he was spending from 1800 hours to 0600 hours on the 27th in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how I understood it. That's what I understood him to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your last explanation, you said or you referred back to paragraph 20 of your statement, again claiming that Nik Peraj is lying, because he, according to you, said at paragraph 62 of his statement that he was put up with his unit in this house. Now, I think you've already said that you would -- that he was subordinated to the operations section, and you would not know where all elements of the operation section were located. So I'd like to refer you to paragraph 62 of Peraj's statement to see exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at paragraph 62 of Mr. Peraj's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the entire paragraph, so could you focus in on that, please, paragraph 62. Next page, please, page 12. I can't see the entire paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read that sentence, the sentence -- the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The house in which the meeting was held, and where during the NATO conflict my department was located, belonged to a Kosovo Albanian; and before the funeral of Milutin Prascevic, it was used by the group plan -- the Meje planning group together. Also based there with my section was elements of the military police. Stanisic's own house was near the barracks of Sadik Stavileci Street."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what you're saying in paragraph 20 is also, I put to you, not correct. Nik Peraj did not say that he was put up there with his unit. He said his department was located there, and you would agree with me that his section, operations section, was a different section from the section that you were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we do move on, let's take a look at which of the two questions that Mr. Stamp asked the witness was the answer that the witness gave, what questions it referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the question at line 24 has been answered; and if there's something else you wish to ask the witness, you will have a chance to re-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your experience in the VJ, have you ever seen a report written about an action or an operation during the course of that action or operation; that is, before the operation or action had ended?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any report about that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not speaking about a specific operation, or maybe I should take you to -- to the paragraph where I'm speaking. We're at Paragraph 22 of your statement. I think you have a copy there. You said it was illogical to report losses in an action that had not yet been completed, and what I'm asking is this: Are you saying that one can -- that in the VJ you can only report on an action or an operation after that action and operation has ended? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I say is that it is illogical for me to compile a report on losses first, because I was not in a position to do that, to compile reports about any actions which referred to the operative part of the brigade command. So we're talking during combat action. And it is also illogical that if something is ongoing and if it lasted for some time, that I would write something about it without any knowledge to do that and information, because I had no knowledge or information that something was happening at that time or what was going on. What could I know in the basement of the cultural centre about what was going on in that action, and, finally, what Peraj himself could have known, for that matter, if he was with me that evening at 10.00, as he claims he was. He says that he saw me making a list of that kind or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What your statement is saying is that it is illogical that you would be making a report on losses because the action had not yet been completed.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I want to know whether or not that it was the standard in the VJ, that there were no -- no interim reports can be prepared during the course of an action. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, bearing in mine the responsibility that I had and duty performed, and I said that I dealt with morale and information and not the operative side of things, the practice was that once an action had been completed, then a report was compiled. You might ask for some supplements or additions, but I didn't know about that for this particular case or for any other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when the action in the Reka-Caragoj Valley was completed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I heard about the action only in 2002, under that name, of course; when the Milosevic trial started, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if you didn't know when the action had been completed, how did you say in your statement that it is illogical that you could be making this report on the evening of the 27th when the action had not yet been completed? You see, you're representing here in your report that you knew then that the action had not yet been completed. The question is this: How can you say that in your report? How can you represent that you knew then that the action had not been completed when you're saying you only discovered about the action a year later?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite resolute that the name of the action is something that I learnt about in 2002. Now, as far as the action itself is concerned, I knew as far as the brigade commander informed us about it. I knew that much. He supplied us with the information that, on the 27th and 28th, an action would take place - he didn't say what the name of the action was - in which a smaller portion of the units would take part in blocking off an area, setting up a blockade in a given area. So, on the 27th, I had this meeting where the Chief of Staff of the brigade command, as far as I remember, informed us that as far as our unit is concerned, and I'm talking about the 52nd unit, that it was evolving according to plan, that there was no shooting from either side, and that it continued the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, sir, are you saying now that you knew about the action in April of 1999? On the 27th of 1999, you knew about the action?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the brigade command, I was informed in the area that the brigade commander thought he needed to inform us, on a need-to-know basis; but I wasn't given any assignment in respect of this action, so it was just general knowledge and information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As the officer responsible for information, would it not be part of your responsibility to send up information about losses incurred in the course of actions by VJ units?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I said a moment ago that we didn't have any losses, nor did we open fire. There was no reason, nor did anybody order me to. So I didn't have the right to send out information on my own initiative, only pursuant to orders from the brigade commander or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last thing on paragraph 22 of your statement I wish to ask you about, if you -- if you have it there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you must have other things to ask this witness about, and we're running out of your time very quickly. I hope it's a question worth asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the last thing in respect to Nik Peraj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphones are picking up an awful lot of noise in the courtroom, thank you, if it could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 22 of your statement, can you read the last sentence -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Read the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. "In addition, it is obvious that Peraj gave a full statement, because I never prepared and created any report for the staff of the 3rd Army in Nis, because this is in collusion with the rules of subordination. "In fact, this would mean skipping the chain of command because we sent reports to the Pristina Corps command, never to the 3rd Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 83 of Peraj's statement, can you read the first sentence of paragraph 83.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 27th of April, 1999, after 10.00 in the evening, I was in the brigade headquarters at the cultural centre in Djakovica. Major Zdravko Vintar, who was employed in the personnel office, was preparing a report for the 3rd Army staff in Nis." Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate for the record that there is -- there appears to be an error in the B/C/S translation of the statement. The original signed copy by Peraj has a report for the Pristina Corps. If we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't there a necessity for the brigade command to meet frequently with the MUP and the municipal authorities in order to coordinate the activities during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember with respect to the MUP, the brigade command did not meet frequently. And if somebody did meet, it might have been the liaison officer of the brigade -- command. Anyway, I did not meet with the MUP. As far as the local authorities are concerned, we did have contacts with them; and on the basis of their requests, we could provide assistance in taking care of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I have one moment to consider whether or not I have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You've not quite exhausted your time yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may use this moment just to draw the Chamber's attention to something Mr. Stamp pointed out, an error, but I think he was mistaken when he said that the original statement was taken in English. I think the Trial Chamber should pay attention to the following: The statement clearly reflects that both English and Serbian were used, English and Serbian. Nik Peraj only speaks Albanian and Serbian. He actually speaks no English; therefore, I think the original statement was done in B/C/S. He gave evidence before this Trial Chamber in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It might be a procedural matter. The original statement, though, is done in English because the investigators wrote and prepare the statement in English. I think, at the end of the statement, it is indicated that it is then -- the English statement which the witness signs is then read back to him in his own language, and he signs the English statement based upon the verification of the interpreter. I think that is the certificate you'll see by the witness and by the interpreter at the back of the statement. Then the statement is -- the written statement is translated into Albanian and Serbian as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not an ideal arrangement. Your point, though, from paragraph 22 is that there isn't a reference to the 3rd Army in the statement but a reference to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, can you think of a reason why Peraj would lie about you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that someone exerted pressure on Peraj because he remained in Djakovica. He continued to live there with his family. So he simply had no choice but to state some sort of a reason, including me and this notorious list, which never really existed, not the way he describes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why you? Did you have a feud over something with Peraj, or did you not get on with each other?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got on just fine. After all, I met his wife once, and he met mine. I was treating him in a respectful manner. My general attitude is that I'm a very social creature. I like talking to people regardless of their religion or ethnicity. All of my experiences were very favourable. I think someone was leaning on him, and he had to keep in mind the benefit of himself and his family, so that's why he ended up saying what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Very brief. I would just like to draw Chamber's attention to one thing and to answer Mr. Stamp about what he said about the translation being authentic. There's one thing that I wish to raise. When Peraj was testifying, which he did both in his statement and viva voce, he was asked whether he'd read the statement. He'd read it in the Serbian language, and he had made no amendments. But in the transcript, if you go back to the transcript, you will see what he said orally about this report and who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When do you claim he said he had read the Serbian statement? When he was in court here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, because he was asked a question, just like we question our witnesses, and the question was did they go through their own statement, "Did you have a chance to read it?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that would be shortly before he gave evidence in the trial, and indeed in the Milosevic trial. So it wouldn't be at the time of the statement initially being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about our trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the point I was making and the criticism I was making was that it's not satisfactory, entirely satisfactory, that at the time these statements are taken, they're taken in English, signed in English, when the native language of the witness is a different one, and it's only later he signs a version in his own language. That's what happened with Peraj, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree. I do agree, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Vintar, can we please look at Exhibit P1086. A very short sentence there that I'd like you to read out for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a translation error, Your Honours; therefore, I think the witness might read it for it us, and I think the page was shown by Mr. Stamp. This is the war log of the 52nd Rocket Artillery Brigade. In order to locate the B/C/S, in e-court, the B/C/S is page 10 and the English is page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, be so kind, please, read this sentence where it says "KM" -- or rather, to have the whole sentence, "Between 1800 and 2100 hours ..." Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Between 1800 hours and 2100 hours, the command post was moved from Marsenic house to the cultural centre in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I think that's quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is something missing in the English. There is one word missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please read slowly. Does it not say "the command post from the location [Realtime transcript read in error "lot case"] of Marsenic house"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the general area around a house. It could be an agriculture land. It could be some sort of a centre or an area, piece of territory. It doesn't necessarily mean that this was actually in the house itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a part in the transcript that's incomprehensible to me. Line 23, 24: "Does it not say the command post from 'lot case' of Marsenic house." Can you deal with that again? That doesn't have any English meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's why I sought explanation. The witness read that "the command post was from the location of Marsenic house," and I asked the witness to explain what this means, "the location."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again, we'll require a formal CLSS translation of this passage in light of the varying answers that have been given and the fact that this answer has emerged as the result of a leading question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours -- well, all right. The witness read "location," and I asked him what that meant and then he explained what that meant. I don't see that there was anything leading about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, this surname, "Marsenic," is that an Albanian surname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Bakrac. I don't want to be unfair to you in any way. Now you show me where in English there is an answer that includes "location" before you put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, and you can listen to the tape, read this because that is what the Serbian says, the text. He read "from the location of Marsenic's house," and this was not translated, "location." Then I asked him what that meant, "location." You can check the tape and hear. In the Serbian, it's very clear: "KM, from location of Marsenic's house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be the case. But in your quieter moments, if you would just read lines 23 and 24 from page 25, you'll see what I mean. Now, just please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, am I right if I say that this document shows that, as of the 1st of April, your office was in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, thank you for this answer. My previous question was about the surname Marsenic. Is that an Albanian surname?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, you told us about this office. The Prosecutor asked you whether Peraj could have any other tasks. I'm asking you: Where was Nik Peraj's office?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nik Peraj's office was the same as mine. We shared an office, and I did say this a couple of times as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could Nik Peraj have or did he actually have another office, or just this one?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nik Peraj had no other office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vintar. I would just like you now to look at P2253. There may be a translation error involved. The Prosecutor asked you to read paragraph 62, the last sentence, which says that: "In that house, together with my detachment, there was stationed also the members of the military police." So, what I'd like you to do now -- you don't have that in the B/C/S yet. All right. Can you please look at the first sentence and read it out loud for us slowly, paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was at a meeting when the massacre at Meje was being planned, because that was going on in the same building in which I was stationed with my unit which was in charge of security."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, you read exactly what he said. Where was this unit that was in charge of security station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that some of the time the -- for some of the time the unit was stationed in the barracks itself in the shelters and for some of the time in the cultural centre, and that was not his unit. He was an officer from the brigade command, and he was in charge of controlling and monitoring its work. He was not a commander. He was not able to have his unit. He was in charge of monitoring, and this unit had its own commander who was in charge of that unit. He was in charge of no more than monitoring, same as me. He monitored their work. He directed their work, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying this unit was in different places at different times, but your office throughout was in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was any part of that unit ever stationed in an Albanian home?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours, for your patience and understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Our next witness is Sergej Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a change of order?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is a change of order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood the next witness was Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Gloncak was supposed to be next, but I might as well use this moment to say that we encountered a problem. On the 14th of January, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We can cope. It's just so that we can rearrange the paperwork. I don't have my statement for Perovic here. I'll just need to arrange to get it brought in if that's the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does present a problem for us because we were prepared for Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our notification --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Gloncak may be in the building already. He arrived by plane last night, but I proofed him last night. I did my best, and I think he's ready to give evidence. If, indeed, he's already in the building, it is all right for me to have him appear first. But why this situation? He arrived last night at 7.00. He's ready to give evidence. We did some work last night just in order to avoid wasting time, but that -- at 10.30, he should be here in the building in ten minutes and he will be available to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the problem about having Perovic now, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can proceed. That's Mr. Stamp's witness, and he'll be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's have Mr. Perovic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just in the interim just indicate to counsel through the Court that there is one administrative problem, in that I should be sending to the Defence now the document that I might use in cross-examination. We're sending a list now, but the document that are not filed or been settled and there may be one or two documents which is not on the list being sent now which might be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you may have got lucky then, Mr. Stamp; but, yes, we can all simply note that, and you can do your best to produce the list asap.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, good morning. Would you kindly state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sergej Perovic. I'm a professional member of the army of Serbia in the rank of lieutenant-colonel. My station is the Nis Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Please appreciate that since we are speaking the same language, you need to make a second's pause before you start answering; and if I make a pause, that means I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, is it the case that to the Defence team of General Lazarevic, on the 8th of January of this year, you gave a written statement?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to review that statement, read it, and sign it?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does it reflect everything you have stated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It fully reflects everything I stated to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, is it the case that, on the 23rd of January, you had the opportunity to review, again, your statement?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you notice that, in two of the paragraphs, certain corrections and modifications needed to be made?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask the usher to assist me. I have this supplemental information. I believe you have instructed my colleague, Mr. Cepic, to prepare the supplemental information in Serbian, and you will instruct me. In paragraph 10, there was a typing mistake regarding the number of an exhibit. I don't know if it's necessary for the witness to read this, but we noticed that instead of 5D1149, the number of the exhibit should read 5D889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 11, Your Honour - sorry - should be modified inasmuch as the number of exhibits that the witness talks about are omitted. I would like the witness to read the paragraph as it should read, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are just examples of you providing the missing information, which is gynaecological reports of 5D1383 and 1384, and that the report -- sorry, the indictment is 5D890. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. That and another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nothing else needs to be filed on that. These alterations we will simply insert onto the copies of the statement we have ourselves, and the record will reflect the alteration. Well, on reflection, yes, because the statement's filed, yes, it's better if you file also the supplementary material under the same exhibit number, which is 5D1396.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe it will be done shortly. We have both versions, English and Serbian, prepared. May I ask to tender this later when we have this supplemental information; that is, 5D1396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, we have your statement, and there is no need to go back to it or to repeat the things stated in there. I have just a few additional questions to put to you in relation to the testimony of Witness Nik Peraj. In your statement, you have already stated that you knew Nik Peraj. You explained how and since when, and there is no need to repeat these details. Thus, Witness Peraj, in one part of his statement, said that you, Sergej Perovic, had told him that nothing would happen to his family during the action in Caragoj Valley on the 27th and the 28th. Are these allegations correct? Did you tell him anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: The allegations of Nik Peraj in his statement, that I had told him that nothing would happen to his family during the action in Caragoj Valley, are not accurate. The truth is that I never had a discussion with him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, have you ever told Mr. Nik Peraj that in order to go to the area where the action would take place he needed a permit?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I never said to Nik Peraj that in order to go to the area of the action he needed a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, have you ever had in our possession a mini map of the action that was carried out on the 27th and the 28th of April in the Reka valley?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I never had any sort of map concerning the action in the Reka valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 27th or perhaps the 28th of April, 1999, did you go with Nik Peraj to Duzanj, where allegedly the command post of the police was located?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th or the 28th of April, 1999, I did not go with Nik Peraj to the area of Duzanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, you told us that it was not correct that you had told Mr. Peraj that he needed some sort of permit or approval or permission to go to the area of the action. On the 28th of April, in the morning, did you go with Nik Peraj to the forward command post of the Pristina Corps to seek such approval or permit?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, I met -- I met up with Nik Peraj that morning in the centre of Djakovica town, and then he asked me to go together to a place overlooking Osek Hilja, which was the area a part of our unit was deployed, that is, the 52nd Artillery Brigade of Anti-aircraft Defence, so he could see what was happening around his house and that he would be able to see his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have all that in your statement, Mr. Perovic. All I want to know is whether he wanted to see what was going on in his village by going into the village itself, or he wanted to see it from some other place.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Nik Peraj wanted to see what was going on in his village by observing from a location overlooking Osek Hilja village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that morning that perhaps he had been alone to the forward command post of the Pristina Corps to seek such approval or permission?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. He never told me anything about seeking permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You served in the security organ. On the assumption that it was correct, what Nik Peraj said, would you, as chief of security in the 52nd Artillery Brigade, and considering who Nik Peraj was and in which position, would you have been simply able to walk into the forward command post, especially if the commander was there?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: The system of security of the forward command post, specifically in Djakovica, did not allow for anyone to come in uninvited into the forward command post. It was necessary for a party or a person to be announced to the security of the outside perimeter after which they would be announced to the security at the reception desk, and only then, with the approval of the person who was receiving, would this party or person be able to enter the premises of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, after the war ended, did you ever hear from Nik Peraj in relation to a house?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: After the security forces were withdrawn from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, I did not hear from Nik Peraj again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were all my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Perovic. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I will have some questions for you briefly, hopefully. First of all, sir, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I apologise. Mr. Perovic, do you recall, in 1999, a meeting in Djakovica with both Generals Aleksander Vasiljevic and Momir Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That meeting took place in the period from the 1st until the 5th of June, 1999, at the Djakovica Garrison. Apart from those two, there was also the chief of security of the 3rd Army, at that time Colonel Stojadin Antic, now deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, General Stojanovic testified here about a meeting between -- about this meeting and the allegations or information that in Djakovica there was a group called Legija commanded by Colonel Kovacevic. Specifically, General Stojanovic, at transcript 19833 lines 19 through 23, said, and I quote: "At that meeting, he was given the task by General Vasiljevic of checking whether any such unit existed and to report to me. After a few days, because Major Perovic then said that this was unverified information, after a few days he reported to me that he had not obtained any information indicating the existence of such a group." Sir, do you recall receiving such a task from General Vasiljevic to inquire about this matter and report to General Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I was given the assignment to check the veracity of those allegations, which I did. I spent a few days trying to establish the possible truth in this allegation; and after that, I informed Colonel Stojanovic that I was unable to confirm these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear before the break, and I think I'll be done after that: Am I correct that you could not verify any of the several allegations raised at this meeting with Generals Vasiljevic and Stojanovic relating to purported crimes by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I was unable to verify any of the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour, and I think we have time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Perovic, we have to have a break at this stage. That will be for half an hour. Would you please leave the courtroom meanwhile with the usher, and we'll see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were born in Djakovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was born in Djakovica on the 3rd of February, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And prior to 1999, you had lived most of your life there?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1985, I'm talking about the secondly military school, a military gymnasium in Belgrade, up until 1988 I attended that school. Between 1988 and 1992, I attended the Belgrade military academy, and I was also in Zadar and Sarajevo for the academy. After I had completed the military academy in 1992, my first posting was at the Kosovska Mitrovica Garrison. In 1996, I was transferred to Pristina, and after that to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks for the detail, but can I just ask you to focus on what I asked; and if you could answer it short and precisely, I would be grateful. As the --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- chief of the security organ for the 52nd Artillery Brigade at the Djakovica Garrison, you received information about events in that municipality from many sources, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: My work was about obtaining information that had to do with my unit which was stationed in the Djakovica Garrison -- or rather, the information that might have affected the safety and security of the unit or its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, isn't a little bit more than that? You also were duty-bound to seek out and obtain information that might relate to the detection and prevention of organised and individual crimes by army members, which is what your statement says. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I gathered information on any criminal offences or crimes that were committed wherever members of my unit were concerned, wherever members of my unit committed those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And General Vasiljevic did say that you -- you were known to have reliable operational sources in the field. Would that be your own assessment of the situation you were in, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the implementation of tasks of my functional duty, I had sources for gathering information within the unit and to a smaller extent outside the unit from the -- across the territory. There were several Albanian persons who were involved in this. At any rate, all the units in the Djakovica Garrison had their own security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware of which VJ units were involved in the action or operation at Caragoj or Reka valley on the 27th and 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I know that in addition to our unit, the 52nd PVO Brigade, that was involved in the blockade of the sector where the terrain was being searched, there were also units of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade. This was a battalion. A component of the 125th Brigade was also involved in the blockade of this sector where the search was being conducted, and that is as much as I know. Those were the units that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you not know that units from the 52nd Military Police Battalion were involved?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military police battalion unit was also involved; one of their platoons or two possibly. I'm not entirely certain about this, though, because this was not part of my work. Therefore, my answer is yes, I'm aware of the fact that military units were involved in this action, some of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were units -- and, you know, this is in Djakovica municipality. That was your -- that was where you gathered intelligence and information, so that is why I am asking about this. Were units of the 63rd Parachute Brigade involved, 63rd Parachute Brigade from Nis?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of. This wasn't my assignment. It wasn't my duty to know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Probably, they had their own security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether there existed at the time a unit called the 63rd Parachute Brigade that was originally located in Nis before it was resubordinated to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that a unit called the 63rd Parachute Brigade existed in the Nis garrison, but I'm not aware of the circumstances concerning its possible resubordination or its whereabouts during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could look at your statement. Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel could help with a copy of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring to paragraph 30 of your statement. You have it there. Can you read paragraph 30?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 30: "The allegation of Peraj Nika, referring to that fact that I told him where the location was of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, or rather, that this brigade was carrying out operations in its Caragoj Valley, I emphasised that I never told him that because I knew nothing about that. Also, the Yugoslav Army never had any airborne landing brigade within its composition, so it is quite obvious that he invented this."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But it was clear -- clearly indicated that he was referring to the 63rd Parachute Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I assume he meant that. Yes. I assume he meant the 63rd Parachute Brigade, because there is no 63rd Airborne Landing Brigade, or rather, to be more precise, Your Honours, I don't know what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is an Airborne Landing Brigade if it's not a Parachute Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No such name was ever used. No brigade was called that. There is a Parachute Brigade. As for this name, there was no unit by that name in the VJ at the time, Airborne Landing Brigade. No such unit existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if you meant what you said. You said when you spoke about this brigade, you don't know what he had in mind. That is what I see here. I am at a loss to understand how it is that you don't know what he had in mind, yet you aver in this statement that based on what he said, you were not speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp. Would you be able to or do you think there's any difference between a Parachute Brigade or an Airborne? Don't you think they are the same thing? It's only a twist on the name. So why don't you kindly clarify it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's clear, is it, or likely that when Nik Peraj referred to the 63rd Parachute Brigade, he was referring to the brigade that participated in the activity at Caragoj Valley on the 27th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You nodded, but you need to verbalise or speak.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he had in mind. I assume it was that brigade he had in mind, because there is no brigade that is called an Airborne Landing Brigade. So I assume that that's what he meant when he was talking about how I had told him all of this and all of these circumstances that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- are contained in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the Parachute Brigade, and this comes directly to what His Honour inquired, would a Parachute Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was perfectly clear. There is no way he can know what Witness Peraj had in mind when he said that. He said it twice already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, please, you will have a chance to re-examine the witness. Do not prompt the witness from your place in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't you understand that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He doesn't seem to know. What on earth does a soldier think an Airborne Landing Brigade is? Did they throw them out the planes and let them drop? What other means is there of getting to the ground than a parachute? Tell me. Maybe there is. Let me know. I'm a layman in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, so am I, but my understanding is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's here the answer from the witness and not from you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Your understanding of a Parachute Brigade, is it of personnel who are airborne and who, by way of or by means of a parachute, land somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Parachute, yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say twice, twice that you don't know what -- what Peraj meant. How is it, if you don't know what he meant, you can represent to us that what you are saying was a fabrication?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: What I said was I assumed that he had the Parachute Brigade in mind. I did not know anything about the Parachute Brigade. I knew nothing about their whereabouts or activities; therefore, I could not possibly have provided to him any sort of information in relation to that. I could not possibly have provided any information to him about what he asked me in that context. I told him nothing about the whereabouts, about the operations, or the tasks of the 63rd Parachute Brigade simply because I was not aware of any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Peraj said, if we could move on, that on the 27th of April, 1999, he went with you in the afternoon to Meje where he saw, and you would have seen as well, four dead bodies at a MUP check-point, and that check-point was close to Sokoli's house. Do you recall seeing that afternoon with Peraj these four dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not see those four dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I think I might have misquoted. He said: "The check-point was in front of the store of Krist Sokoli just opposite the school." That's paragraph 69 of his statement. Do you know the store of Krist Sokoli?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that you both that afternoon moved on in Meje and went to the vicinity of Hasanaj's house where there was a check-point; and there, there were the dead bodies of 20 men. Did you see that that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: That day I did not enter the combat disposition, because when we came to a certain sector -- or rather, the beginning of the area in which the search was being conducted, the members who were there turned us away saying that we could not access the combat disposition -- or rather, this area where the search was being conducted because we were no members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No members of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the combat disposition. I'm asking you about a police check-point in Meje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp. I just want a clarification. Sorry for this interruption. When the witness says, "We could not access the combat disposition," could you kindly inquire from him what he means by the word "we"? Does it mean that he was with Peraj or can he say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Were you with Peraj that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had every intention of going to his home; however, we were stopped from doing this, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The operation -- the evidence before the Court, and I don't want to have to go into maps now, is that the operation was in the Caragoj Valley from the top in terms of elevation in the Junik village right down to Meje and Korenica at the end near Djakovica. So I'm not asking about the combat dispositions up in the valley.
