I'm simply asking you about Meje at the bottom of the valley, whether or not you saw the dead bodies of 20 men at a police check-point.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I would like to add this: This was no check-point. There were a group of people there that we came across, a group of persons, members of that unit. This was no check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was no check-point? I didn't identify a check-point. I just spoke. Maybe there's something wrong with the check-point. What are you referring to when you there was no check-point?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the question of Mr. Stamp, he says "check-point." So I don't know what kind of linguistic problems we're having here today, but it's driving me bonkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer was: "This was no check-point," and I certainly don't understand what that is referring to either. It seems to be a specific location; whereas, the question was much more general and that's the point that Mr. Stamp is trying to clarify, and I would welcome his clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you clarify, or would you like the question repeated?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your specific question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about whether or not you saw 20 bodies at a police check-point. You are referring, it seems to me in your answer, to a specific check-point. Is that what you are doing? Was there a specific check-point that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any dead bodies next to the check-point you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Which check-point are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you were asking me about whether I saw any dead bodies in the vicinity of a check-point, and that is the only reason that I'm referring to a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Do you know where Hasanaj's house is?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Nor do I know anybody called Hasanaj, if you're talking about a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of 20 dead bodies being found in the vicinity of the bus station in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you report to General Vasiljevic about 20 dead bodies that were found at the bus station in -- in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the report you mentioned. I don't think so. But I know that I did inform him about the activities of the previously stated group, the alleged activities of the previously mentioned group in the Djakovica area. I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible that you could have made a report to your general, Vasiljevic, about 20 dead bodies and forget about it thereafter? Is it possible that you could have made that report and have now forgotten about making that report?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I wrote anything about these specific 20 dead bodies at the bus station because I don't remember it, and I think that I would have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Vasiljevic seemed to be quite certain that not only you reported it to him, according to his testimony, but you were aware of it yourself. I think I will just read what General Vasiljevic said on the transcript at 9034: "But he," and he's referring to you, "did have reliable operational sources in the field who relayed this information to him. But as far as the bodies at the bus station are concern, I think there were about 20 corpses there, and he knows about it well." That was his impression that he got from you. Now, are you saying that not only is Nik Peraj being untruthful about your being present when bodies are located but so is General Vasiljevic about your report to him? Is General Vasiljevic lying when he says that you reported that to him?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we're dealing here with two different locations altogether. In the first part, we're talking about Meje and some man called Hasanaj; and in the second part, we're referring to Vasiljevic and the bus station. So they're not the same things at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's quite clear, and you say you don't know anything about either. Mr. Stamp is asking you if that can possibly be right in view of what General Vasiljevic said when he was here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presented and I said what I said. Now, what Vasiljevic said, whether he already had some information about that and just asked to test this in talking to me, which is not essential at this point, but anyway, I think -- or rather, I did not give him that information about the 20 corpses at the bus station in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, if you became aware of significant crimes, war crimes, murders, rapes committed against Kosovo Albanians by security forces in the course of an operation where VJ units, including units from your brigade, were involved, and when I say "operation," operation or action where units including your brigade or from your brigade were involved, would it not be your responsibility to thoroughly investigate those allegations?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Had it been my duty that if some members of my unit had committed a crime or there were any indications of the fact that members of my unit had perpetrated a crime, then it would, indeed, have been my duty to look at all those indications and have all the operational data, which was not checked out, to have it checked out and then to report to my superior officer within the frameworks of which a more detailed investigation would have been organised. Of course, let me stress, if they were members of my unit who were concerned. So my operative remit and responsibility was for my own unit and also for the risks involved and that could have an influence on the unit's security and its members in its area of deployment. So much from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you have information that Kosovo Albanians are killed in a action where your unit is -- and you were unit is involved in the action, wouldn't you be responsible to investigate the allegations of the killing?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: If it was perpetrated by my unit, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't know if it was perpetrated by your unit --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Or are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would not know it was perpetrated by your unit unless you investigated it. That's why I asked the specific question. If there are allegations that people are killed or serious crimes are committed against persons during an action in which your unit is involved, would you not have to investigate those allegations of killings to see whether or not your units were involved in the killings?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I was duty-bound to establish all the circumstances which could influence -- or rather, which would indicate that the perpetrator might have been somebody from my unit, the perpetrator of anything that could be in contravention of the conducts of an army and soldiers. Now, if I were to establish that it was, indeed, one of my members, especially if it was -- if the crime happened in my area of deployment, then this would be an indicator to me to take steps to conduct an investigation in the manner which I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if it, your investigations, established that the crime was committed by members of the MUP, would it not also be your responsibility to report it and take steps to see that it was followed up by the appropriate organs?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I personally, as a security organ of the unit, did not have the authority to implement my operational work vis-a-vis the MUP organs. However, if I were to have any knowledge whatsoever about any criminal acts, crimes, then I would be duty-bound to inform my superior officer thereof -- or rather, up the chain of command, my chief --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- in order to establish what was true and what was not of the allegations made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you conduct any investigations into allegations of crime, serious crime, against civilians in the Caragoj Valley during the 27th, 28th, and the 29th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge of the crimes mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your answer you are saying that you did not conduct any investigations in respect of that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I did not have any information about that, nor --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- did I conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it further, that the VJ, to your knowledge -- or withdraw that. May I put it this way: Are you whether or not the VJ conducted any investigation in respect of crimes committed during actions in the Caragoj Valley on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I do not know whether the army of Yugoslavia -- or rather, the leaders of the VJ knew about any of this, the then army of Yugoslavia, about the crimes mentioned. But I did not know of them, and so by the same token I did not inform my superior of the existence of any crimes, but within the frameworks of my unit. Similarly, I did not inform him of the existence of any crimes in the area. I didn't report to him about this, nor did I mention any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say -- let me see if I understand you. You didn't see the bodies Nik Peraj said you saw. You didn't make the report about the bodies to General Vasiljevic. Did you receive any reports from any of your sources about the disappearance of over 300 Kosovo Albanians from the Caragoj Valley area on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a security officer with the reliable sources that General Vasiljevic spoke about, did you receive any information as to where these bodies were concealed or any information as to how they were disinterred, transported, and re-buried at Batajnica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As the chief of security for the Djakovica Garrison, how -- how could you miss this, or is it that you will not testify about crimes, the crimes committed by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've never heard of this type of question being asked. I'm speechless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it that you will not testify about crimes allegedly committed by the MUP in the valley?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say is wrong with that question, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the question was -- he's giving two options: Is it this or this? He needs to separate it into two questions, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's now separated. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're not going to testify about allegations of crimes committed in the valley by the MUP, are you? You don't know of any?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I do want to testify about anything I know, but I have no knowledge that anybody perpetrated any crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you are -- withdrawn. I'll put it this way: You said that you were unable to verify any of the crimes that you discussed with General Vasiljevic. This is a general question: Do you know of any serious crime committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians by the MUP during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that there were two questions in that. Now, shall I answer the latter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I'll rephrase that: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've only got one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There was, but I think the witness is adopting what Mr. Ivetic had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any serious crimes committed against Kosovo Albanians by MUP units during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. I don't know. I heard of some, but only afterwards. I heard that there were indications from the information media and so on and so forth, but I didn't know about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Or more exactly, I heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We heard from a witness, Hani Hoxha, that on or about the 23rd -- 27th of March, 1999, while he was at his home in the Kula quarter in Djakovica, Serb security forces, amongst the police, entered the area, fired shots in the neighbourhood, burned houses, and expelled people. Did you receive any information about that event at -- at any time during the intervention?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We heard from him and Lulzim Vejsa, that is say, Hani Hoxha, that on 1st and 2nd of April at Qerim district, at house 157 Milosh Gilic Street, Serb police burnt the house to the ground killing 20 of the occupants, mostly women.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Perhaps I'm wrong, Your Honour, but I don't see how this part of the cross-examination has anything to do with the examination-in-chief. The witness heard Milos Obilic, instead of the correct name, which was Milosh Gilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your point, but the cross-examination does not have to have anything to do with the examination-in-chief. It just has to be relevant. So just please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't hear of a property on -- at 157 Milosh Gilic Street being burnt to the ground resulting in the death of 20 people, 20 Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Even now, at this moment in time, I'm hearing that for the first time about that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We had a witness here who was a member of the military police battalions that were involved in the action on the 27th, and he said that he travelled with his unit down the mountain -- or down the valley on the 27th and 28th of April, and houses were burnt and people were expelled. You said, in your statement, that you went to some elevation so you could look down into the valley on the 28th. Did you not see any of these houses burning?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: On that 28th, as I have or already stated, I was at the top of that elevation above the Osek Hilja village, and I stayed there for about ten minutes. Visibility was good, very good, that's true; but at the time, I did not see any burning or any smoke or any fire, and I didn't even hear anybody firing, any shooting. I stayed there for about ten minutes, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nik Peraj, I think you're aware, has described you, so far as he knows, as a good person. I think he said a good man who saved many lives and that he always maintained good relations with you. He indicated and he went out of his way to express very high regards about you and your conduct. Now you come and say that he is lying when he speaks of you being present when he saw these bodies. Do you have any reason why he would lie on you or speak these lies about you?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I wish to stress that I was -- up until that time in 1999 when he stayed in Djakovica and I left the area, left Kosovo and Metohija and the Djakovica Garrison, we had good and proper relations. Now, I was surprised to hear the quantity of untruths which he stated in referring to me, even if it was the simple kind of thing and sentence that said, "I told him something which happened," which did not, and so on. Now, the reason why he's doing this, I don't know. I can only assume. It is my assumption -- or my assumption relates to the fact that he, as a member of the army, was blackmailed in some way by members of the KLA after leaving the security forces in Kosovo and Metohija. Since many members of his family stayed on in Kosovo and Metohija, most probably he had to accept that blackmail and give the kind of statements that he gave. That's my personal assumption, but I think that that's why he acted in the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But any concrete reason why you? Do you know of any concrete reason why you, apart from that assumption?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't say. He mentioned other members of the army with whom he had good and proper relations otherwise, so I don't know why he singled me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, at the time, what was your understanding of the outcome of the Reka action?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, within the frameworks of my authorisations and powers, I collected all possible knowledge and information about shooting and actions towards my unit and coming from my unit within the frameworks of the duration of the said action, and I informed my superior officer thereof. Now, since the other units had their security organs, I did not have the authority to gather information for those units. Well, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm assuming that no matter what role precisely you play at any given time that when there's an action being conducted where you're forming a blockade in support of that action, that you're likely to find out what happened. Are you telling me you didn't find out what the outcome of this action was?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I found out about the result of the action, the outcome of the action, within the frameworks of my unit, that is to say what my unit did, but not the other way round, coming towards my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, did you learn that there was -- I'll start that question again. Did you learn that homes were being searched in the course of the action?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what did you understand was involved? You're forming the blockade. What did you understand that others who were actively involved in the conduct of the action were doing?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about my unit. As for members of units which conducted the search of the area, I have no specific knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had you no idea what the police were doing, for example?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is an intervention in the transcript, 58, 3 and 4. I don't think that the witness said exactly what is in the transcript. It's a bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What he has said is actually that: Within the frameworks of my unit, that is to say, the shootings from my unit and shootings towards my unit." That was the -- that was the essence what he had in -- in his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. Two or three questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Perovic, we were discussing the participation of the 92nd -- sorry, 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade in this action called Reka on the 27th and 28th. Tell me, please, how many troops performed a blockade from your unit, and what kind of unit was it, from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: The blockade was performed by a force three-platoon strong, equivalent to around 60 troops. The 52nd Brigade, the Rocket Artillery Brigade of Anti-aircraft Defence, was responsible for the anti-aircraft defence support to units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment ago our colleague, Mr. Zecevic, intervened and corrected something in the transcript. You said that you knew what your unit participating in the blockade did and what activities were aimed at your unit. Did your unit open fire, and was fire opened at it?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: That unit did not open fire, nor was there any fire opened at its members, those who were in the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. You were asked about Djakovica, about the town itself. In the town itself, as far as you know, was there any fire from the KLA, and was there any battle, combat, with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: From what I remember, there was sporadic fire targeting members of the army and members of police units in the town itself, in some of its parts, specifically in a neighbourhood called Novi, which it was, meaning a new part of town. But as for frequent sporadic fire, individual and in groups by Albanian terrorists, was more concentrated in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have one last question. You have graduated from a number of military schools. Tell me about airborne landing units around the world. Do they also have tanks and artillery?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do they transport tanks and artillery by cargo planes as part of their force?

utterances.speaker: SERGEJ PEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Perovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Franjo Gloncak. Your Honours, perhaps this is a convenient moment. This will be our last witness for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now going to duck, are you? We'll look at the position in relation to that, once we've heard from Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gloncak, good afternoon:

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you state your for the record? Your full fall name, date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: My name is Franjo Gloncak. I was born in 1952 in Palic, Subotica municipality. I currently reside in Nis which is about 600 kilometres away from my birthplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, I will not have many questions. My examination will be brief. Would you kindly make a brief pause after my question and speak more slowly so that the interpretation may be correct. Mr. Gloncak, is it correct that to the Defence team of General Lazarevic you gave a statement on the 26th of December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review that statement, read it, and get familiar with it -- with its contents?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that statement reflect what you said, and did you sign it in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I signed it in my own hand, and it reflects what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today again, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Defence Exhibit 5D3095 [as interpreted], and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, I will have just a few questions and clarifications to seek from you and possibly an additional question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher's assistance in giving one copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, can I confirm that his statement is Exhibit number "5D1395" as opposed to "3095" that's appearing in the transcript right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it is 1395.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my learned friend Mr. Hannis. I meant to correct it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So Mr. Gloncak, in paragraph 8 -- or rather, let's deal with paragraph 7 first. You spoke there of an incident when Pirane, near Prizren, was bombed, and you said in paragraph 8: "The army extended assistance to these people." Whom did you mean when you said "the army?"

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Of course, in that area, it was the area of responsibility of the 549th Motorised Brigade from Prizren. When I said the army extended assistance, I meant the members of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Below, in paragraph 11 of your statement, you spoke of another incident when the NATO bombed a column of civilians near Korisa village, and you said that among several members of the army, I suppose your own unit, you too went to donate blood at the hospital. You noticed, on that day, a large number of doctors and other medical personnel of non-Serbian ethnicity. Were there any other ethnicities and who?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That day, when I donated blood for the victims of the Korisa incident, I believed that there were more than a hundred victims of thermal bombs that targeted that column. Apart from that medical personnel at the hospital in Prizren, the victims were assisted by our own military doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, in paragraph 13 of your statement, you spoke of airstrikes on the Gorozup-Planeja axis in a stretch of five to six kilometres. You said that carpet bombing covered all the settlements in that area, Ceja, Planeja, Ninaj, Binaj, and Seh Mala. What does that mean, "carpet bombing"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That means that the entire area on our side of the border, which was the direction in which the offensive of the terrorists went, was targeted by carpet bombing from strategic bombers, B52, and all these settlements were wiped out. Even the foundations of the houses was turned into powder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, if I understood you correctly from your statement, your son, before you joined the army after the NATO airstrikes began on the 24th of March, 1999, was doing his regular military service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which unit was he in?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: My son was doing his military service from June 1998; and from September onwards, he was in military post box 4445, which means 444th [as interpreted] Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it should be 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with your son before you joined this brigade yourself?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was in touch with my son in several ways. We wrote to each other; we contacted by telephone that was available for that purpose, for families to be able to contact soldiers; and I visited him personally two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he share with you his experience of the army, his views on the army and of his superiors, his officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What was his experience with his officers and the corps command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: His experience was, if I can sum it up in a few sentences, that the training is intensive, that the discipline is very firm, that officers are strict, but that they take good care of them, conscripts doing their regularly -- their regular military service. He didn't only say that about his immediate superior officer. He had that same opinion of the entire brigade command, I'm sure, and the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he tell you of the prevailing opinion of -- among the troops and the officers of the corps commander, General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His opinion and the opinion of other members of the brigade was very high of the command and General Lazarevic specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about your personal experience once you joined the brigade? Was it the same as your son's?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: What he told me and what he communicated to me in other ways was confirmed from my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You are a member of the Association of Veterans or fighting men. What is the prevailing opinion today among them of the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: He still enjoys today, as then, their confidence, and he is held in high esteem. You didn't ask me, but I want to say that I worked for a long time in Kosovo as a travelling salesman. I still have contacts with ordinary people, including Albanians. I never heard anyone say anything bad or negative about General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there another Defence cross-examination? No. We have to break at this stage, Mr. Gloncak, and resume in an hour at quarter to 2.00. Meanwhile, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose we should address your question, Mr. Bakrac. You say this is the last witness. You never know. He might occupy the afternoon for all we know, but perhaps that is unlikely. You have one other witness available, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that one more witness who is here arrived last night at 7.00 p.m., together with the current witness. I suppose that you know the name and that we don't need to go into private session. It's a severely disabled person; and when I saw him last night, he said he was extremely tired from the trip and that he was unable to talk. As I said before, from 7.00 p.m., I nevertheless proofed Mr. Gloncak additionally until late last night. I don't want to shift blame onto anyone. But on the 14th of January, we asked those five witnesses: Zdravko Vintar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about the arrival of everyone, but I was simply asking you to explain why it wouldn't be possible to take the witness who is here and we'll consider what you say. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about your statement. Do you have a copy of it on your table?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, you tell us about when you first served in the army and that you stayed until 30 October 1982 and transferred to the reserve force. Why did you leave the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: At one point in my life, I believed that I would be more successful in other areas, in other jobs, and I was looking for a chance to do something else for a change.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand from reading your statement that -- that you worked for a while as a sales representative for different furniture factories; and in paragraph 3, we see that in July 1998 you were called to a military exercise. Between 1982 and 1998, did you have any active duty in the army or were you simply in the reserve that whole time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I was in the reserve, which didn't mean that I wasn't called upon to do my job with the Territorial Defence in Nis from time to time. I was the commander of the signals platoon, and it went on like that until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. We read in paragraph 4 that after the -- the bombing started, you joined the army as a volunteer on 25th of March, and you mention when you did that you went through some testing, including a psychiatric examination. What did that consist of? Was that a written test or an oral test? Exactly what was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Psychiatric, is that the only thing you have in mind, that examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only one I'm asking you about right now.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: There was a person, rather, two persons from the military hospital in Nis, two psychiatrists, and they checked everyone who volunteered to join the defence forces of their own free will. First, there was a written test; and after that, there was an interview with one of the psychiatrists. They would check your reflexes, that sort of thing, whatever it is that they do; and, of course, motivation was one of the things that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How long a written test was this? Is this something that took days or hours or half an hour?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The written part took one hour, and the evaluation itself with all its other components would normally take an entire day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You tell us that you were first sent with a group volunteers to the 175th, and you arrived there at the end of March. So I take it, then, that you were there until you got transferred to your son's brigade, the 549th, which you tell us in paragraph 5 was around the 4th or 5th of April. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was with the 175th for four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where exactly did you go when you got transferred to the 549th? You told us you were stationed in the surroundings of Prizren. Can you tell us exactly where you were?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The exact whereabouts of the unit that I was transferred to at this point was a farm, an agricultural farm, next to Dusanovo village in Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that called Ekonomija?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible to call it that. There was some agricultural machinery and some livestock there that was bred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5 you mention, you say: "During those several days that I spent in the surroundings of Gnjilane and then in Prizren..." I'm not clear, sir, from your statement. When were you in Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Zegra. That's the place near which I was. I spent those four or five days near that village, and this village is in Gnjilane municipal territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you're referring to the time when you were with the 175th?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you. Now, I'd like to show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a photo. It's Exhibit P3047, and this is a photo we showed when General Delic was here to testify. If we go to the second page, please. It's from a book by a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the cover page, but I want to show you the photograph. I don't know how well you can see that on your screen, but this is purported to be a group of volunteers who fought with the 549th; and on the top right of the picture standing on the stairs, if you come down to the third person there, General Delic told us that was -- that was him had. Can you recognise him there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: On the right-hand side from the top down, the third person in uniform is General Bozidar Delic. He was a colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the other people in this photograph until?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I've never been to this place, and I wasn't there with this group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Even though you've never been there, have you -- do you recognise any of these people from anywhere else during the time you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 6, you mention that you saw several examples of -- of NATO bombing, and you said you can mention some about which you have personal first-hand knowledge. By my rough count, I think you describe six or seven different incidents, but it's only the first one, in paragraph 7, on 15 April 1999, in the village of Pirane that it seems to me that you were -- you were actually there. Is that right? You were -- you witnessed that one on the 15th of April with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's true, and I also witnessed the strikes on Prizren, the airstrikes. Prizren was teeming with civilians on the 1st of May. As for the airstrikes that were carried out against the refugee column near Korisa, I wasn't there when the airstrike occurred, but I was there to witness the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk some more about that in a minute. But this first one in paragraph 7, you mention that between 1400 and 1500 hours that day, these Albanian civilians on tractors were bombed, and you say: "As I estimated from a distance of about 500 metres, with a Mark class air bomb ..." So if I understand correctly, you're at a distance of about 500 metres away from where the bomb struck the civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right, with another three persons. The distance between us and place where this occurred was about half a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't actually see any aeroplane from which this bomb came, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I saw an aeroplane. It was an F-16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were able to see the bomb at a distance of 500 metres and determine that it was a Mark class air bomb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Based on my experience and based on the effects of the same bomb that I saw in other places, I still believe this to have been an M-82 missile, bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- you're -- you're not a bomb expert. Your military speciality was in communications; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 9, you tell us about a second case that happened on the 1st of May from around 2030 hours to 0030 hours. The town of Prizren was heavily bombed. You say it was full of civilians. When you say Prizren was full of civilians, you don't -- you don't mean it was exclusively full of civilians, do you? I mean, there were also MUP and VJ personnel in and around Prizren on that day; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were members of the army and the police there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what - and you'll have to excuse my pronunciation of the Serbian - but can you tell me what the Cviljen feature is? I understand it's some kind of communication device or building or structure, the repeater?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph are we in, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got it now in paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The name of the feature, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cviljen is a hill right next to Prizren, and there was a repeater at the top, for telephone communications, TV, and radio. It was a civilian installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, approximately, how far from Prizren is it located, and in what direction?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The distance between Prizren and Cviljen is about three kilometres, as the crow flies, to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the Car Dusan Silni barracks? Those were located in Prizren, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The Car Dusan Silni barracks is far from Cviljen. It's at the other end. It's when you leave Prizren and head towards Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far from the town or city limits of Prizren were the barracks located?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: To all practical intents, it's on the outskirts of Prizren town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in Dusanovo, there were VJ artillery weapons located, were there not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I saw no artillery units in Dusanovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what about artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I show an exhibit, 6D1004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can give you a hard copy, and I'll ask you to go to page 5. You can look at the first page first. This is dated the 6th of May, 1999. It's a Republic of Serbian Ministry of Interior report for information obtained in the period between 30 April 1999 and 5 May 1999. I assume you've never seen this before, have you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you go to page 5, and in English it's at the top of page 4. In your copy, sir, I've highlighted something in pink, and I'll read it out and ask you a question. It says: "The constant targets of NATO aircraft in this period were the already mentioned Cviljen repeater, the Car Dusan Silni VJ barracks, and in particular the positions of the Yugoslav Army in the village of Dusanovo in the immediate vicinity of Prizren." And at the very end of the paragraph, it mentions destruction to some homes in the village of Dusanovo and VJ artillery weapons located in the village. Now, were you not aware some VJ artillery weapons were subjected to NATO bombing during the week of 30 April to 5 May 1999? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and I don't. I don't think this is the case. It can't possibly be the case. There were no artillery weapons or units in Dusanovo next to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a problem in the transcript. Can I ask my learned friend or the witness to read the last portion of the paragraph that Mr. Hannis was showing to him. It is not my intention to anticipate the actual answer, but I think it has been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you want to do on this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the witness read the last part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the part that is marked out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can read the whole -- the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: "At this period, the Cviljen repeater that I've mentioned, the Car Dusan Silni VJ barracks, in particular the positions of the Yugoslav army in the village Dusanovo, were constant targets of NATO aircraft, and this is in the immediate vicinity of Prizren. During those airstrikes, an enormous material damage was inflicted, especially by the destroying of over 40 houses in the village of Dusanovo. Also, a number of private agricultural facilities or farms were destroyed as well, as a number of VJ weapons were stationed in that village." It should be "that were stationed in that village."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does it not say "artillery weapons"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: When we talk about "artillery weapons," we mean artillery weapons. During those airstrikes on those days, some weapons were destroyed that were part of the LAD PVO of the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. My question is, though: In my English translation, it says "artillery weapons." Is that what says in Serbian? Can you confirm for me or read it again, because when you read it this time it just said "weapons," but I understood that it says "artillery weapons." I'm just trying to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: "Artillery pieces."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What was the -- what was the name of the unit that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're going to have to re-examine on this, Mr. Bakrac. You'll have the last opportunity to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Gloncak. Can you tell me what was the name or the number or designator of the unit that you were assigned to in the 549th?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: It is 2787/61. This is a LAD Artillery Rocket Battalion of the anti-aircraft defence, and it was part of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you another exhibit. This is P2575, and it's described as a war diary of the Light Air Defence Rocket Artillery Battalion of the 549th. That sounds like your unit, but maybe you can have a look and tell me if it is. You can't tell much from that first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to start at page 8 of the English, and it's page 8 of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gloncak, I'd like you to take a look at the entry for April 7th. It's item number 16 in the handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to enlarge the left-hand side of this document, and I don't know if -- do we not have English in e-court? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, can you see that entry for the 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go down, I think it's -- I think it's about two-thirds of the way down on this page. There's a reference to the 3rd Motorised Battalion taking up positions in Dusanovo village. Do you see that? It makes a reference to a location 700 metres west of Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read that sentence out loud for us, since we don't apparently have the English here.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Is that the one that starts with the time indication, 1920?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: "At 1920 hundred hours, after the support was completed, the 3rd MTB in these villages took up positions in Dusanovo village sector 700 metres west of the farm and carried out preparations to conduct," probably it says "anti-aircraft combat. "The quartermaster's detachment -- squad is..." You want me to go on reading that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can stop there. Thank you. Do you recall seeing this unit set up about 700 metres west of Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I didn't see them the moment they deployed, but I knew that the unit had been transferred. But can I tell you what I think this misunderstanding is about, Mr. Prosecutor? You talk about artillery pieces, guns, Howitzers, --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have limited time. Mr. Bakrac may be able to ask you some questions again when I'm finished. I want to go back to your statement. You mentioned another incident on the 1st of May in Prizren, and then you mentioned in late April and early May when NATO was bombing around the area of the repeater on Cviljen. You mentioned going through a village of Lokvice. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that when you went through, there wasn't -- that it was inhabited exclusively by Muslim inhabitants and nobody had -- had left. Is this a Gorani -- is this a Gorani community? Is that the right term?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I don't think these are Goranci or the Gorani community. I think these are Muslims. I didn't even want to know then or now. What I'm saying is they weren't Orthodox or Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you mentioned there were four Orthodox churches in the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right. There were in that village until the time we left Kosovo. I don't know what has since become of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess I'm not clear. The village was exclusively Muslims, but there were four Orthodox churches and one mosque. Does it mean that there were no Serbs living there? Were these Muslims who were Orthodox by religion?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No. There is no such thing. Those places of worship are far older. The make-up of the local population had probably changed over time, but people cared for these buildings enough to preserve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take a look at a map to look at the Prizren area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at P615; first of all, page 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, I'm going to show you a map that purports to show basically the -- the city or the town of Prizren. Can you -- can you recognise that, what's on your computer screen or should we enlarge it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I can see it, but I'm not an expert in town planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. From your time there, are you able to tell us that this generally is consistent with the -- with the layout of the town of Prizren? You see the railroad tracks on the left side running from bottom to top of the page. Does that help orient you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it certainly does. I can see the basic contours now. I can see the main passage and the railway tracks. Yes, that is Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would the -- the Car Dusan Silni barracks be on this photograph or are they farther away from the town, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The barracks, the Car Dusan Silni barracks, should be outside this map but very close to the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Dusanovo would be sort of outside this map near the top left, correct, sort of following along the railroad tracks?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Yes. The red route leading up left is the Djakovica-Prizren road, and it is on that road that the village of Dusanovo lies. Of course, it can't be seen on this section of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 22 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try to show you a map that's zoomed out a little bit, Mr. Gloncak, and see if you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could enlarge the lower right quadrant that has Prizren. Maybe one more time even. Can you see that, Mr. Gloncak? Do you see Prizren in the lower right corner?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know see where Dusanovo is written on the map here? It actually appears to be --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I do see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you -- the usher will help you. We have a pen there where you can actually draw on this map. If you could mark a number 1 with a circle in it to indicate approximately where you were located.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we give that an IC number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I think I drew it in too low down, too far down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll give you a clean one and start over again if that's possible. We'll give you a clean one, Mr. Gloncak, and give you a chance to mark again. If you could just put a little number 1 and draw a circle around it. We understand it's approximate.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all you're getting, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a little more now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we give that an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gloncak, I wanted to move on to one the other NATO bombings you talked about. In paragraph 11 of your statement, you mentioned hearing about something near the village of Korenica -- or Korisa on the 14th or 15th of May. You weren't actually there. This is something you heard about over the radio at the time; and then later on, you found out some more information about it; right? But you weren't there first-hand, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see. You mentioned around -- in paragraph 12 of your statement, around the 29th of May, you remember a convoy of civilians bombed on the Prizren-Brezovica road before Recani. Again, this is not you personally witnessed, is it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No. I wasn't an eyewitness of the bombing either on the first day of the Cviljen column or the Portuguese news crew or the British.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, you talked about the 29th of May and the carpet bombing. You said all villages on that axis, Ceja, Planeja, Ninaj, Binaj, Seh Mala, et cetera, were covered by a carpet bombing. You didn't personally see that at the time it happened, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I was right near those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you list five villages there and you say "et cetera." How many additional villages do you include in this event?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Those were the villages and hamlets that were in that area. Nine years after that period of -- after that, I really can't remember all the names of the various little places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you remember a number? Are you talking about just one more for a total of six? Are you talking about 12 or 20?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No. They're not that many in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And over how widespread an area are you talking about? Can you give us an estimate of how many kilometres or square kilometres you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: As for the breadth, I think it's an area of around four to four and a half kilometres. It does not mean that the carpet bombing engulfed the fields, meadows, but the settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know, do you, whether or not there were any VJ or MUP personnel or equipment or weapons located within the area where the bombs were dropped, do you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: There were units of the army there. I don't know about the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us earlier today when you testified - it's at page 64, line 3 - beginning at line 3, you said: "All those settlements were wiped out. Even the foundations of the houses were turned into powder." Are you telling us that in all of those villages over that entire area nothing is left but powder? That's an overstatement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a slight exaggeration, but the countryside did look like something on the moon, and there was total destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't take any photos, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No. I did not have a camera, nor did it occur to me at the time to take souvenirs of that type back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned, in paragraph 16, you say: "Many civilians told me that in addition to fear from NATO bombing, they were also leaving because of pressure exerted by KLA members." How may civilians are you actually talking about? How many civilians did you personally speak to about that issue, fear of NATO bombing and pressure by KLA members? Are you talking about five people or 50 people, a hundred people?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the figure could be around 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you talk to those 50 people?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Over a longer period of time, we're talking about the beginning of April onwards up until the end of May roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: On the territory that I moved around in and where I met people, came across people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these are Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Not only Kosovo Albanian civilians. I also talked to the Gorani and to some Turks and, of course, to the Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What percentage of these 50 were Kosovo Albanians that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Well, let's say three-quarters roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in your VJ uniform at the time you spoke with them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Of course, I was. It was my duty to wear my uniform at all times, just as it was the duty of all other members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you think that they might be hesitant to tell you, a soldier in a VJ uniform, that the reason they were leaving is because they were afraid of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Well, it was wartime. That's possible, too, but what I'm telling you is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. You say in that same paragraph: "I know that KLA members carried out the massacre in the village of Rogovo because Albanians from that village did not want to obey their orders to move out." First of all, can you tell me, approximately, when that massacre was that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I didn't go to that area. The source of information was in talking to people from Rogovo, and the village of Rogovo should be located to the north of Prizren somewhere thereabouts, bordering on the Djakovica and Orahovac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mention, in paragraph 17 of your statement, I think when you were in the Zegra area, that you saw two or three conscripts maltreat and seriously injure an elderly woman. You told us they were immediately arrested and escorted to Gnjilane. According to what you found out later, they received prison sentences of 14 years each for this. I will tell you we've had a number of witnesses here, from military judges and prosecutors from the VJ, who brought in a number of reports of those VJ members charged with crimes and sentenced. I'd like to ask you, first of all, how did you go find out about these guys? What was your source of information about them getting 14-year prison sentences?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I talked about that to a member of the 175th Brigade after the war, several months after the war, and I think he was an officer in that brigade. We happened to meet. He was a captain by rank. I remember that, and I remember his nickname, Jovance [phoen]. The man lives in Leskovac to that day. That's less than 50 kilometres away from where I live, the town of Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And these conscripts, were they also from the 175th?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That evening, as volunteers, together with a group that I had arrived with, they arrived in the broader area around Zegra. They directly violated orders not to enter the village and not to enter the houses, and I saw them with my very own eyes being taken away by the military police, handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question, I think, was: Were they members of the 175th, or assigned to the 175th brigade? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: When we arrived in the brigade's area of deployment, of course all of us were included in the composition of that brigade. We were already a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your only source of information of about them receiving a prison sentence of 14 years comes from this captain whose nickname you gave us, right? You didn't see any media accounts or see any court records about what happened to them, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see anything in respect of that case or any other, because it wasn't what I was interested in job-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Gloncak. Those are all the questions I have for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I just wanted to advise you that the English translation, Your Honours, of that diary for the Artillery Rocket Battalion is now available in e-court in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, during the period of the war, what particular actions, combat actions, by the VJ did you take part in?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Specifically, I took part in combat action during the Strela operation, the attack which began at the end of May along the axis of the Gorozup border hut and the lake there, Planeja, Ceja, the place I mentioned, and it was an attack towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you were part of a combat unit at the time and in the area of the carpet bombing that you described to us.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the time of the bombing, was there fighting in process?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. The infantry attack from the territory of the Republic of Albania was already under way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who do you say made up the infantry attacking from Albania?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: They were the forces of the armed rebellion of ethnic Albanians, as you call them, but I would say terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, earlier in the period of the war, were you involved in any active combat?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: My VES was signals, so I did take part in many of the elements of the work of the defence forces. You asked me about direct combat, and I answered that question. VES being military occupational speciality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as a signal operative, if that's what you were called, did you also in that role participate in other actions during the war, albeit you were not wielding a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which were these actions?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: It was organisation of anti-aircraft defence, where there are separate points with whom communications were maintained; and when the need arose, I had to do other work on technical maintenance, electricity, the establishment of communications where they had been severed, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you connected in any way with any other action against the KLA or any other terrorist body?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Only in one case did I take part in refuting an infantry attack from the village of Vladovo in the period when I was deployed in the 175th Brigade. That was a short period of shooting which went on for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were there casualties?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Not on our side, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the other side?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it only the VJ that were involved or were there other groups apart from the VJ involved?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Only the army of Yugoslavia -- or rather, members of the 175th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who was your opponent?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: On the other side, it is the assumption that they were the forces of the Albanian terrorists or rebels, insurgents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did that action come to an end?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: I don't think it was actually an action but provocation on their part. During the night shooting, we returned fire, and that's where it ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And apart from the matters you've dealt with in response to these questions and your involvement in Strela mentioned in the statement, is there no other planned action of the VJ that you were in anyway involved in, either in your duties as a signalman or in an active combat role?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: If the so-called PVO ambushes are included in those actions, the ones you have in mind, then yes. PVO, anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say "PVO ambushes." Is that a correct translation of what was said? Well, what do you mean by an anti-aircraft ambush?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Yes. I meant anti-aircraft defence ambushes where an anti-aircraft defence weapon is put out into the terrain waiting for an overflight of an enemy aircraft in attempt to take it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were your anti-aircraft weapons also used against targets on the ground?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Those weapons could not be used against targets on the ground. It's a launcher, Strela 2 or Arrow 2, which is exclusively intended for combat against aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything arising from that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, and we have to clarify one error in the transcript. I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, Mr. Gloncak, you said something about it in your statement, what happened to your family house during the war?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: The house where I was born, it's actually a resort at Lake Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be suggested, I think, by Mr. Hannis that that doesn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it does, because I believe a whole series of questions of Mr. Hannis had to do with destroyed houses and whether they were destroyed because the army was there. My next question was whether the army were stationed or based in his house at Lake Palic. I believe Mr. Hannis questioned about bombing of civilian facilities that the witness is aware of, and he tried to suggest that everywhere around such buildings there were army troops. I believe it does follow from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour. I don't see how that relates. I ask about houses that is were destroyed in Dusanovo near where he was stationed and artillery pieces were stationed. I don't see the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, you can ask questions about houses in areas which Mr. Hannis dealt with, where you think the suggestion has been left that there were military targets in these areas; but beyond that, it would not be appropriate to go arising out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, all these examples of NATO airstrikes and buildings destroyed, were they exclusively military targets from what you were able to see and assess, or were they civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Indiscriminate bombing by NATO is what I think. It's not only military installations that were targeted. It was mostly civilian facilities that were targeted. May I correct myself? Mostly civilian facilities were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 6D1004. Can we have page 5, please, in B/C/S. Can we zoom in, please, on the second paragraph. Just a minute. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gloncak, you've already read this paragraph. I would like to know in the last sentence -- or rather, in the entire paragraph, but especially in the last sentence, is it written anywhere "artillery weapons"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: It says "orudje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It means artillery weapons, but the witness says it says only weapons.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO GLONCAK
utterances.text: Although, the Prosecutor suggested to me artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance to all, so we don't lose the time. I think that the most adequate translation of it would be "pieces of weaponry." That's "orudje," pieces of weaponry. It is not artillery pieces, although it is used also for artillery pieces. But in Serbian language when you say "orudje," it can be mostly anything which belongs to the army; and if it's artillery piece, then it says "artiljerija orduje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will not have arguments, personal arguments, across the courtroom. If you have a submission to make, make it, and Mr. Zecevic should be allowed to make his submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to -- to be of assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may not be any of your business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It appears so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I think, Mr. Bakrac, what else happens in your re-examination, we shall require reconsideration of the translation of this part of page 5 of 6D1004 by CLSS who will make a report; and if you have a submission to make about it, you can make a further submission. But there may be other questions you would like to ask. There certainly is one I would like to ask of the witness, which is this: There is no disagreement amongst anyone here but that the reference is to weapons. What weapons do you understand that that refers to or have you just no idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you that. I was trying to when the Prosecutor told me there was no more time. What he says was destroyed, the artillery pieces of the VJ, is not artillery pieces. It is an anti-aircraft weapon of the army of Yugoslavia, a combined cannon mounted on a vehicle called Praga with two barrels. It is not an artillery weapon. It is an anti-aircraft defence weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I dare say to Mr. Hannis that he would probably have classed that as an artillery weapon; perhaps not. That may be the question answered, but you'll have a chance to comment on the translation issue when the translation is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, and I believe it would be useful, perhaps, to listen to that segment of the tape when he read it, but I don't think we should waste any more time on that. With this explanation, the witness now said what he intended to say when he was stopped. I believe it was about Exhibit P2075. I don't think we need to open that exhibit. Those would be all my questions. Thank you, Mr. Gloncak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Gloncak, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The information we have in relation to your next witness suggests that we ought to grant your motion to postpone hearing him until Monday, which we shall do. There has been some information relayed to us by VWS at my request which suggests not ideal communications about the arrangements for attendance. So I think for the avoidance of doubt, we don't need to get into any dispute about that. I'm not for a minute suggesting that it's all your responsibility or that there's any need to attribute fault here, but there was clearly a breakdown in communication. But for the avoidance of doubt, there is every possibility that all your witnesses will be required next week. So you have to bear that possibility in mind and consider carefully with VWS your arrangements for the attendance of witnesses, so that we make full use of the time available. All right? So we will adjourn now until Monday at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic.
